items.title: From bias to bots: discrimination and AI service preference
items.abstract: Purpose While artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled services have become increasingly prevalent, little is known about how discriminatory service encounters influence consumers’ preference for AI-based service providers. This research aims to investigate whether – and why – perceived discrimination in human service encounters increases consumers’ preference for AI-driven service options. Design/methodology/approach Three studies were conducted to test the proposed framework. Study 1 used an autobiographical recall design, Study 2a experimentally manipulated discrimination, and Study 2b used a 2 × 2 between-subjects experimental design. Mediation and moderated mediation effects were examined using PROCESS. Findings Across the three studies, perceived discrimination was associated with greater preference for AI service providers through reduced social comfort with human providers and enhanced perceptions of AI ethicality. Cultural tightness consistently strengthened the social-comfort pathway, whereas its moderating influence on perceived AI ethicality and the direct effect was less consistent. Practical implications The findings offer actionable insights for designing inclusive service systems, deploying ethical AI solutions and enhancing customer experience strategies. Originality/value This research shows that human–AI service provider preference is shaped not only by the attributes of the available providers but also by consumers’ treatment in a preceding human-delivered service encounter. By linking discriminatory encounters to subsequent provider choice, the study extends research on service encounters, AI-enabled service and service inclusion and offers a socio-psychological explanation for why consumers may develop a stronger preference for AI-based service providers.

items.title: Functional Sequelae of Musculoskeletal Trauma and Return to Work: Occupational Capacity, Disability Assessment, and Medico-Legal Integration
items.abstract: Musculoskeletal trauma may produce persistent functional sequelae that extend beyond anatomical healing and significantly affect occupational participation. This study analyzed the relationship between post-traumatic musculoskeletal impairment, residual functional capacity, occupational demands, work incapacity, return-to-work outcomes, and medico-legal assessment through an integrative review based on the Scientific Method. Evidence from traumatology, rehabilitation medicine, occupational medicine, functional capacity evaluation, and medico-legal literature was examined to identify the principal clinical, functional, psychosocial, and occupational factors associated with delayed or incomplete work reintegration. The findings showed that persistent pain, reduced mobility, muscle weakness, decreased endurance, functional limitations, injury severity, self-efficacy, educational level, physical workload, occupational category, and recovery expectations influence return-to-work trajectories. Functional Capacity Evaluations provide useful objective information regarding work-related performance, but their interpretation requires comparison with actual job demands and integration with clinical, psychosocial, and contextual factors. Workers whose residual functional capacities were compatible with occupational requirements demonstrated more favorable return-to-work outcomes, whereas persistent capacity-demand mismatches were associated with unsuccessful reintegration. Workplace interventions, including modified duties, ergonomic adaptations, coordinated rehabilitation, and graded return-to-work programs, were associated with improved initial and sustained occupational outcomes. From a medico-legal perspective, the evidence supports a clear distinction between anatomical impairment, functional limitation, occupational restriction, and disability. Work capacity should therefore be determined through an interdisciplinary and individualized assessment integrating objective sequelae, functional performance, job-specific requirements, prognosis, rehabilitation potential, and workplace adaptability. This multidimensional framework provides a more precise and defensible basis for disability assessment and for planning safe and sustainable occupational reintegration after musculoskeletal trauma.

items.title: Generative AI & Two Forms of Decoupling
items.abstract: Textual artifacts are sometimes valued not only for the words on the page, but for the human activity involved in producing them. The effort invested in a carefully tailored email can signal genuine interest; composing an apology might involve attending to another person's hurt and deciding how to respond; and requiring a judge to give written reasons may induce more careful deliberation. AI models create what we call a decoupling problem: they make it possible to produce text without undergoing the relevant human activity, severing its connection to values traditionally sustained by that activity. This Article develops a framework for understanding what decoupling puts at stake, and how institutions that use text to make consequential decisions may reshape their practices in response. First, it offers a taxonomy of the grounds for valuing the production process, distinguishing whether that process matters for what it evidences, induces, or helps constitute. Second, it argues that text can function as a kind of boundary object, allowing institutions to rely on the same artifact without resolving disagreements about why the practice is valuable. AI can separate functions previously served by the same practice - a second-order decoupling that brings unresolved questions about the practice's purposes into view. Third, it argues that institutional efforts to repair decoupling may recover some functions without preserving others. Such responses are likely to favor functions that are more legible, whose loss demands immediate attention, or whose stakeholders have greater influence. It therefore calls for more explicit deliberation about which particular functions of a practice to preserve, with meaningful representation for those whose interests might otherwise be overlooked.

items.title: Generative AI communications and firm value: Evidence from digital innovation in tourism, travel, and hospitality firms using deep learning
items.abstract: This study examines whether firm-initiated generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) communications are associated with firm value in UK-listed tourism, travel, and hospitality (TTH) firms. The final sample includes 177 firms from 2018 to 2024, comprising 68 firms with verified WeChat official accounts and 109 firms retained with zero-valued communication measures. From 105,429 archived posts, we develop a bilingual annotation scheme and supervised deep-learning classifiers to identify GenAI communication and distinguish implementation-salient disclosures from generic mentions. Our preferred measures are share-normalized, capturing both GenAI communication intensity and implementation emphasis relative to total posting activity. Firm- and year-fixed-effects results show that implementation-weighted GenAI communication is positively associated with Tobin's Q and operating performance. Digital innovation partially mediates this relationship, while industry dynamism and complexity strengthen it, but munificence does not. The study contributes a tourism-specific measure of GenAI capability signaling and clarifies the value relevance of implementation-oriented communication in service-intensive digital contexts.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Writing Pedagogy: Challenges, Ethical Concerns, and Future Directions
items.abstract: Particularly in terms of supporting writing, artificial intelligence can now do much more. It alters children's reading and writing skills as well as teacher evaluation of their work. Apps that help with language, programs that offer quick feedback, and tools that generate text are all examples of AI that can provide helpful advice, rapid responses, and additional writing practice for students. These fresh technologies provide problems even if they are beneficial and help to save time. Problems with honesty in schoolwork, excessive reliance on computer applications, the equilibrium between appropriately utilizing technology and not, and the loss of critical thinking or creativity comprise these. These obstacles are forcing teachers to reevaluate their teaching methods and ensure AI supports student learning instead of merely dominating. Although AI in education has some limitations and challenges, its potential to be enormously beneficial in the classroom is also quite high. This piece discusses more on how these difficulties come up while teaching writing. The report demands explicit instructions, suitable teacher training, and substantial school support to effectively apply artificial intelligence in order to enhance education.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Use in United States Doctor of Physical Therapy Programs
items.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education is poised to significantly impact the field of physical therapy. Research on generative AI use in physical therapist education remains limited. OBJECTIVE: The objective was to examine generative AI use in physical therapist education among students and faculty. DESIGN: This was a cross-sectional, online survey. SETTING: The survey was conducted among accredited Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) programs in the United States (US). PARTICIPANTS: Students and faculty were recruited from US DPT programs as of January 2025. INTERVENTION(S) OR EXPOSURE(S): Generative AI use within DPT programs was measured by participant self-report. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: A novel 32-item survey comprising closed- and open-ended questions assessed generative AI use, patterns and purposes of use; platforms, training and comfort levels, views on generative AI's role in physical therapist practice, student preparedness and academic integrity, adoption facilitators/barriers, and demographics. Factors associated with generative AI use were examined using multivariable logistic regression. RESULTS: Among 1067 respondents (873 students, 194 faculty), 853 (79.9%) reported using generative AI, including 687 students (78.7%) and 166 faculty (85.6%). ChatGPT was the most common used platform (662 students, 96.4%; 153 faculty, 92.2%). Common reasons for use included creating study guide/sample questions (482 students, 70.2%; 74 faculty, 44.6%) and creating patient cases (370 students, 53.9%; 102 faculty, 61.5%). Barriers to use included concerns about reliability and scientific rigor (student users: 411, 59.8%; non-users: 133, 71.5%; faculty users: 90, 54.2%; non-users: 14, 50.0%) and lack of trust in the technology and/or companies behind it (student users: 287, 41.8%; non-users: 112, 60.2%; faculty users: 63, 38.0%; non-users: 13, 46.4%). Generative AI use was associated with higher self-reported comfort with the technology (students: OR = 11.6, 95% CI = 7.9-17.1; faculty: OR = 14.3, 95% CI = 5.1-40.0). CONCLUSION: Generative AI is widely used among DPT students and faculty, yet substantial variability exists in its use and formal instruction within DPT programs. RELEVANCE: As its integration into health care accelerates, incorporating education on generative AI within DPT programs is crucial to ensure students are prepared to use these tools competently and responsibly.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Use Practices in the Educational Environment: Experiences of Students and University Teachers
items.abstract: Aim. The study aims to examine students’ perceptions of GenAI technologies and to identify key behavioural characteristics of their use (frequency, purposes and conditions of use, training exposure, and digital infrastructure) associated with positive or cautious attitudes towards these technologies. Methods. The study presents empirical findings on the use and perception of GenAI in an educational context. A total of 120 students and 25 teachers participated voluntarily. The primary method was an online survey designed to capture practices of GenAI use in learning activities and respondents’ attitudes toward its opportunities and risks in higher education. Results. Students demonstrate a higher level of GenAI use than teachers and employ a broader range of tools. Information about GenAI is primarily obtained through informal channels, while the highest level of trust is attributed to academic sources and official platforms. Most students intend to continue using GenAI, which is strongly associated with prior practical experience. A positive relationship was found between the intensity of GenAI use, digital engagement, and attitudes toward the technology. Conclusions. GenAI use in higher education is growing but remains uneven, with higher engagement among students. A positive association is confirmed between usage experience, digital engagement, and attitudes toward GenAI. The technology is mainly perceived as a learning support tool rather than a replacement for teachers; however, risks related to academic integrity remain.
